text:
HR@10 with one positive and 99 unique negatives measures success within 100 candidates; it is not full-catalog HR@10. Sampled metrics can reverse model rankings even in expectation, so gains support conclusions only under the pinned candidate protocol. Smaller candidate sets generally make hits easier; fixing evaluation seed 42 ensures reproducibility but does not remove sampling bias. Keep the evaluator unchanged and label results explicitly as sampled HR@10. [Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

Recommended uncertainty reporting: publish each category’s hits/200, HR@10, and candidate-minus-baseline difference, plus the equally weighted four-category macro-average. Compute a paired, category-stratified user bootstrap: resample 200 users with replacement within each category, preserve each user’s baseline/candidate pairing and fixed candidates, then recompute the macro difference. Report a 95% interval and bootstrap method/count. One additional hit changes category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models, fixed categories and candidates; they exclude training-seed and negative-sampling variability. User-level statistical comparisons are supported by [Cañamares et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-020-09371-3).

Repeated validation-based selection introduces optimism: an ordinary bootstrap interval around the selected winner does not account for adaptive search. Disclose all trials/checkpoint evaluations, search budget, selection rule, baseline and selected configuration; describe validation gains and intervals as exploratory. Keep training seed 42 and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation after selection is frozen. Neither four categories nor one training seed establishes generalization across domains or training runs. [Cawley & Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
